transcript:
Meeting header:
- Date/Time: 2025-06-27 15:00 UTC
- Duration: ~62 minutes
- Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Liam (Redwood SE), Priya (Hexagon Head of ML), Carlos (Infra), Asha (CTO), Julian (DevOps), Nora (Product), Victor (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-gen, may be rough):
Hexagon is evaluating Redwood Dedicated for a 6-week POC to validate reserved GPU pools with burst capacity and safe fallbacks. Main asks: define success metrics (latency & throughput), sizing for reserved GPUs, burst and queueing strategy, failover policy to hosted variants, and security requirements (KMS, audit logs). Action items include Redwood sending POC runbook, security docs, cost spreadsheet and an initial benchmark harness.

Transcript:
[00:00] Maya Ortiz: All right everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE for this account. With me is Liam, our solutions engineer. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Priya Nambiar: Good thanks. We got a bunch of folks from infra and security on the call today. Want to keep this pretty scoped — POC to prove we can run our redaction/triage pipeline with predictable latency.
[00:12] Asha Patel: Hi, Asha here. We're on a short timeline, Q3 pilot we hope. Looking for clear success criteria so execs can sign off.
[00:18] Liam Chen: Great, thanks. Quick agenda: define success criteria, talk workload shape and sizing, POC timeline, and the burst/fallback strategy for reserved GPUs. We'll also touch on security and next steps. Does that work?
[00:25] Carlos Mendes: Yup. Also want to flag; our infra spikes are pretty spiky, like 10x for a few hours during incident ingestion. So burst is critical.
[00:31] Julian Park: And we have strict SLOs on tail latency — 95th under 350ms for small prompts, 500ms for longer.
[00:36] Maya Ortiz: Perfect — that's useful. Priya, can you give a quick sketch of the workload? Average RPS, prompt length, model family?
[00:42] Priya Nambiar: Sure. It's mostly a triage microservice that runs a 3-step pipeline: classify -> redact -> summarise. Models are Llama-2 style open models right now, we expect to test a 13B quantized variant and a 70B float/quant mix. Prompt tokens avg 80-120, sometimes up to 512 for long docs. Baseline steady state is ~15 RPS, peak bursts up to 150 RPS for 30-90 minutes maybe 2-3x/week during scans.
[01:04] Liam Chen: OK that maps to both low-latency and throughput concerns. For POC, we typically propose reserving a baseline Dedicated pool sized for steady RPS and using burst capacity to handle spikes. We need to decide queueing vs rejecting vs fallback to hosted.
[01:16] Victor Gomez: From security we need all inference keys stored with our KMS, audit logs for token-level events, and no model weights leaving our VPC for the POC. Are those doable?
[01:26] Liam Chen: Yes — Redwood Private can run in your VPC and integrate with KMS/HSM. For the hosted fallback we can support encrypted tunnels but we'll call that out as a non-default for POC since you want weights local.
[01:36] Asha Patel: Good to hear. On cost we need an estimate: reserved baseline cost + estimated burst spend. How do you recommend sizing GPUs?
[01:44] Liam Chen: Rough approach: take steady throughput (15 RPS) * avg tokens per request * tokens/sec per GPU for the model and derive GPUs needed. For quantized 13B we typically get ~600-800 tokens/s on T4-like class or ~1500-2000 on A10/A30; 70B is lower. For your 13B-ish tests, a single A10-style instance with concurrency and batching might handle the steady state with headroom. If you want exact numbers we'll run a short benchmark with your prompt set — that's part of the POC.
[02:08] Priya Nambiar: We can provide a sample of 1k requests from last week — Carlos will share.
[02:12] Carlos Mendes: I'll drop logs and a small file. Also our budget is capped; we prefer to reserve as little as possible but ensure we meet SLOs. Burst should be a lower-cost pay-as-you-go.
[02:20] Maya Ortiz: Understood — so strategy: reserved pool sized for 15 RPS with 2x headroom, burst pool to absorb spikes. For failover, couple options: queue with client-side backoff, return 429s, or transparently route to a lower-cost hosted model variant. We can prototype both behaviors in the POC.
[02:36] Julian Park: Transparent routing to hosted sounds risky given data residency. We might prefer queueing with a short retry window, then reject after TTL.
[02:44] Nora Li: Product question — what latency hit do you see when you move to a quantized 70B vs an optimized 13B? We're concerned about quality vs latency tradeoffs.
[02:52] Liam Chen: 70B quantized still higher latency: maybe 2-3x tokens/sec slower than 13B quantized, depending on kernels. We can set model rules so critical short prompts hit the 13B, and longer, lower-priority jobs go to the 70B. That's part of the routing policy.
[03:06] Priya Nambiar: Success criteria we'd propose: 95p latency under 350ms for small prompts on steady state, availability > 99.5 for the pipeline, and cost per 1M requests within X (we'll define X after benchmark). We also want a regression check against our quality eval set, tolerances +/- 2% on key metrics.
[03:20] Maya Ortiz: That looks good. We'll formalize SLOs in the runbook. For availability, Redwood Dedicated has SLA options we can include for pilot length.
[03:28] Carlos Mendes: Can you walk through the burst billing — is burst charged at list price or some blended rate?
[03:34] Maya Ortiz: For pilots we often provide a blended estimate — base reserved charge + metered burst at on-demand rates. For enterprise contracts we can negotiate a blended cap. We'll put numbers in the cost spreadsheet.
[03:43] Victor Gomez: Security follow-up — we need SOC2 Type II evidence, penetration test artifacts, and details on audit log retention and access controls.
[03:50] Liam Chen: We'll share the SOC2 summary and a tech note on audit logs (how they're captured and where they live). For retention, default is 90 days but we can extend for Dedicated. We'll note that in the doc.
[03:59] Asha Patel: Timeline check — what's realistic to get a 6-week POC going?
[04:04] Maya Ortiz: Typical cadence: Week 0 (agreement + infra setup), Week 1 (baseline benchmarks and correctness checks), Weeks 2-4 (stress tests, burst runs, fallback validation), Week 5 (analysis & tuning), Week 6 (final report & exec review). So about 6 weeks end-to-end. If logs and prompts are ready fast we can start infra in 3-5 business days.
[04:21] Priya Nambiar: That fits our Q3 pilot ask. We'll aim to have artifacts to you by 06/30.
[04:26] Carlos Mendes: Quick technical — for queueing, do you do distributed request queue or per-instance? We run kubernetes and want to avoid single points.
[04:33] Liam Chen: Redwood's runtime supports both a centralized queue and client-side retry. For Dedicated we deploy a local queueing layer in the VPC that can autoscale horizontally; no single point if configured with multiple shards. We'll sketch config in the runbook.
[04:44] Julian Park: And what about KV cache behavior across burst nodes? Will you maintain cache warm across scaling events?
[04:50] Liam Chen: We do KV cache pre-warming and prefix caching; during burst we use policy-driven cache sharing or accept cold-start penalty depending on the scaling profile. For your POC we'll test cache warming thresholds and measure tail latency impact.
[04:59] Priya Nambiar: Benchmarks are key — can we do a controlled 2-hour spike test to replicate the worst-case and capture 95/99 percentiles?
[05:06] Liam Chen: Absolutely. We'll run a benchmark harness with varying RPS and token lengths, capture CPU/GPU utilization, latency percentiles, and cost per token. We'll also simulate node failures to validate fallback.
[05:17] Maya Ortiz: I'll include a sample benchmark plan in the runbook and Liam will own the harness.
[05:22] Asha Patel: On fallback — if Dedicated pool is saturated, do you have a circuit breaker so downstream doesn't see long tails?
[05:28] Liam Chen: Yes, circuit-breaker + automatic fallback to queuing or erroring with 429. Optionally we can route to a lower-cost hosted model but only if allowed by data policy. For Hexagon we flagged weights must remain local, so hosted fallback will be read-only summary variant with only non-sensitive data.
[05:42] Victor Gomez: We'll need explicit data flow diagrams showing what leaves the VPC and what goes to hosted.
[05:48] Maya Ortiz: We'll provide a diagram and the security appendix.
[05:51] Priya Nambiar: One more thing — rollout: how do we do canary or percentage rollouts? We want to ramp traffic to Dedicated gradually.
[05:58] Liam Chen: Redwood Console supports route-level traffic splitting, canary with percentage rollouts, and automatic rollback based on latency or error regressions. We'll instrument alerts tied to your SLOs.
[06:08] Carlos Mendes: Good. For the POC acceptance, we'll define a pass/fail matrix: performance SLOs, reliability checks, and security checklist. If all pass, we move to a 3-month reserved contract.
[06:17] Maya Ortiz: Sounds like a plan. Any other questions or concerns?
[06:20] Nora Li: Just to confirm — will you include guidance for quantization profiles and suggested batch sizes?
[06:25] Liam Chen: Yes, the optimize playbook will recommend quantization levels, batch sizes, and kernel choices based on your prompt distribution.
[06:31] Priya Nambiar: Great — that covers most things.
[06:34] Maya Ortiz: Ok final recap and next steps: Maya to send POC runbook + cost spreadsheet by 2025-07-02; Liam to share benchmark harness + security appendix by 2025-07-01; Carlos to share traffic logs by 2025-06-30; Priya to finalize model list and eval set by 2025-07-01. We'll schedule the baseline benchmark for week of 2025-07-07.
[06:53] Asha Patel: Thanks everyone, appreciate the clarity.
[06:56] Victor Gomez: Thanks.
[06:58] Maya Ortiz: Thanks all, we'll follow up in email. Bye.
